855.title: The Wartburg
855.hook: hidden in a castle, Luther translates the New Testament into everyday German
855.howItsDone: Christians across churches read the Bible in their own languages today, and Bible translators still face Luther's question of how close to stay to the original wording and how close to ordinary speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Worms: Luther before the emperor, captive to the word of God, and the emperor answering with his own conscience. Your line was here I stand. Where did you hold your ground, and stay kind? Day eight hundred fifty-five.

A wagon on a forest road, heading home from Worms. Suddenly, horsemen burst out of the trees, drag one passenger out, and gallop off with him. Word spreads that Luther has been seized, maybe killed. In fact, the kidnapping is a rescue, arranged by his own prince to hide him. That night he's taken up to a castle on a hill, the Wartburg. His monk's habit is gone. He lets his hair and beard grow, and the castle staff call him Knight George. And there, an outlaw now, with time on his hands, he picks up the Greek New Testament. Today: the Wartburg.

Luther worked from the Greek text that Erasmus had printed, the one we met a few days ago. And he set out to put it into German, not German bent into the shape of the Latin, word for word, but German the way people actually spoke it. Later, in a letter defending his translation, he explained how. You don't ask the Latin letters how to speak German, he wrote. You ask the mother in the house, the children in the street, the common man in the market, and you watch their mouths as they talk. Then you translate that way, and they'll understand you. He even gave an example. In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Put word for word into German, Luther said, that sounds like nobody's mother talking. A German mother would say something closer to: when the heart is full, the mouth runs over. So that's what he wrote. Not every scholar liked it. Some said he bent the text. Luther pushed back hard. There's also an old story that he threw his inkwell at the devil in that room. It may well be a legend. What isn't legend is the result. His New Testament came off the presses in German that could be read aloud at home, in the language of the market. And the work didn't belong only to Protestants. Catholic scholars produced German Bibles too, and in English, translators like Tyndale were doing the same thing, chasing the words of ordinary speech.

Here's the practice: explain something in plain words. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing you know well that other people find confusing. Your job. A rule of a game. A line of scripture. A recipe your family makes. Now explain it in your head, in the words you'd use with a child at the kitchen table. No jargon. No showing off. If a word sounds like a document, swap it for one that sounds like a person. Say it to yourself until it sounds like talk. If you pray, you can offer that plain explanation as a gift. The bell holds the time.
The Wartburg. The castle where Luther hid as Knight George and turned the Greek New Testament into the everyday German of the house, the street and the market.
Your line: the language of the market. Today, explain one thing to someone in the plainest words you've got, and watch whether their face says they got it. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Katharina von Bora
856.hook: a nun who escaped, tradition says, in a herring cart, married Luther, and ran a brewery, farm and household
856.howItsDone: Lutheran churches remember Katharina von Bora, and some honor her in their calendars of commemoration; her household is often held up in Protestant teaching as a picture of the pastor's family and home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Wartburg: Luther in hiding as Knight George, asking the mother in the house how to say it. Your line was the language of the market. Did your plain words land? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

Behind a convent wall, in the days before Easter, a group of nuns have been reading pamphlets smuggled in from Wittenberg, and they've decided to leave. Leaving is dangerous. A merchant who brings goods to the convent agrees to help. One night his covered cart rolls away loaded with empty barrels, barrels that once held herring, tradition says. Tucked in among them, hardly breathing, are the nuns. The cart makes it out. Among the women who climb down at the other end, smelling of fish, is the one this day is about. Today: Katharina von Bora.

Katharina had been placed in a convent as a girl. Now she was out, with no money and no family able to take her in, and the reformers tried to find husbands for the women who had left. For Katharina, a match was tried and fell through. Katharina, the story goes, let it be known she would marry Luther, or one other man, and no one else. Luther was surprised, and then he did it. They moved into his old monastery building in Wittenberg, and she turned it into a household. She brewed beer. She kept a farm, cows and pigs, a garden, an orchard and a fishpond. She fed students who boarded with them, and refugees, and a stream of guests who came to argue theology at her table. She managed the money, which was not Luther's gift. She nursed the sick. And she raised their children. Luther's letters to her are full of teasing affection. He calls her my lord Katie, putting the word for a lord or master in front of her name. He calls her a rich woman, a doctor, a preacher, a brewer. When he made his will, he left everything to her, which surprised people at the time. The Bible has a poem for a woman like this, the capable wife in Proverbs. In the King James Bible: "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." Catholic and Lutheran readers tell her story differently. For Catholics, leaving a convent broke solemn vows. For the reformers, marriage was a holy calling too. Either way, she is a reminder that a movement runs on someone who keeps the house standing.

Here's the practice: thank someone who runs everything. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose work keeps your life running and mostly goes unseen. Someone who cooks, schedules, cleans, remembers birthdays, pays the bills, keeps the office or the church or the family from falling apart. Let their face come into view. Think of one specific thing they did this week. Not a general thanks. One thing. Hold it, and plan how you'll tell them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them, by name. The bell holds the time.
Katharina. The nun who escaped in a wagon of barrels, married Luther, and ran the brewery, farm and household at the heart of the Wittenberg reform.
Your line: my lord katie. Today, tell the person who runs everything one specific thing they did, and thank them for it, out loud or in a message. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: A mighty fortress
857.howItsDone: Lutheran churches sing "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," and other churches sing it too; Psalm 46 is read in worship and in private prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katharina von Bora, who, tradition says, left her convent in a herring cart, and who ended up running Luther's household, farm and brewery. Your line was my lord katie. Who runs everything around you, and did you thank them? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

"God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." That's the opening of Psalm 46 in the King James Bible. And look at what the psalm does next. It doesn't describe a quiet afternoon. The earth moves. The mountains slide into the sea. The waters roar. By its second verse the psalm is standing in the middle of the shaking, and it says, right there, we will not fear. Martin Luther took this psalm and turned it into a hymn. In his German it opens Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott. In English it's often sung as a mighty fortress is our God. Today: the psalm, and the song Luther built on it.

Start with the psalm, because it's short and strange. Its second verse, in the King James wording: "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed." Not because nothing bad is happening. Because God is a refuge while it happens. Then, right in the middle of all that roaring water, a different kind of water appears: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Floods outside, a gentle river inside the city. And near the end, after talk of bows broken and spears cut in two, comes this line: "Be still, and know that I am God." It comes right after talk of war, not at a spa. Now the hymn. Luther took the psalm's refuge and made it a castle, a fortress with walls. His verses name an old enemy, the devil, scheming and armed. They admit that human strength won't win that fight, and they name the one who fights for us: Christ. A single little word, the hymn says, can bring the enemy down. The last verse is the bravest. In paraphrase: let them take our goods, our honor, even our families and our lives; they gain nothing, and the kingdom still stands. So one psalm gives two pictures. A fortress you shelter inside when the enemy comes. And a river, and a stillness, in the middle of the city. Some Christians lean on the walls. Some on the stillness. The psalm holds both.
screen: `A RIVER IN THE CITY OF GOD.`
`BE STILL, IN THE MIDDLE OF A WAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm 46. It's short, and you can find it in any Bible or on your phone. Read it slowly, out loud if you can. If reading isn't possible right now, hold its three pictures instead. Mountains sliding into the sea. A river running quietly through a city. And the words be still. Notice which of the three you keep coming back to. If you pray, you can let the psalm's first verse be your prayer. If you don't, simply sit with whichever picture stays. The bell holds the time.
Burg. German for fortress or castle, the word at the heart of Luther's hymn on Psalm forty-six, a mighty fortress is our God.

Your line: a river, and a stillness. Today, when something shakes your plans, pause before you react and say the line to yourself, or the psalm's words: be still, and know. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: The small catechism
858.hook: Luther wrote a simple Q&A for families: what does this mean?
858.howItsDone: Lutheran churches use Luther's Small Catechism to teach children and adults, especially before confirmation; Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches teach with catechisms of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 46 and the hymn Luther built on it. Your line was a river, and a stillness. When something shook today, which did you reach for, the walls or the stillness? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

A small booklet, open on a table at home. A parent reads a line out loud: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Then the parent asks a question, the same question the booklet asks after almost every line: what does this mean? And a child answers, in a sentence short enough to remember. That's the scene Martin Luther wrote for. In the preface to his Small Catechism, he describes going around the parishes and being shocked at what he found: ordinary people who barely knew the Lord's Prayer or the commandments, and pastors who couldn't teach them. His answer wasn't a thicker book. It was a thinner one. Today's word: catechism.
screen: `NOT A THICKER BOOK. A THINNER ONE.`

segments.voice: A catechism is a teaching book, usually set out in questions and answers, for learning the basics of the faith. Luther also wrote a larger one for pastors. The small one has a note at the top of each part: this is how the head of a household should teach it, simply, to the family. So the classroom he had in mind was a home. The Small Catechism walks through the Ten Commandments, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer, then baptism, confession and the Lord's Supper. And after each piece comes the same short question: what does this mean? Here's how plain the answers get. The first commandment, no other gods. What does this mean? In Luther's answer, we should fear, love and trust God above all things. That's it. One breath. Or take the Lord's Prayer, "Give us this day our daily bread." What does daily bread mean? Luther's answer is a long list that sounds like a household inventory. It includes food and drink, clothing and shoes, house and home, fields and cattle, money and goods, a faithful spouse, good government, good weather, peace, health, good friends and faithful neighbors, and the like. Shoes and good weather, inside the Lord's Prayer. The question does something on its own, too. It assumes the words you've said over and over might still be closed to you, and it invites you to open them. Lutheran churches still teach with it. Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed Christians have catechisms of their own, each with its own questions and its own answers. But the small question Luther kept repeating is one anyone can borrow.

Here's the practice: ask what does this mean? Choose one line you've said or heard so often it slides past. A line of the Lord's Prayer. A verse from yesterday's psalm. A blessing your family says before meals. Even a saying a grandparent used to repeat. Say it once, slowly. Then ask the catechism's question and answer it in one plain sentence of your own. If you pray, you can end by saying the line again as a prayer. If you don't, just let your one sentence sit. The bell holds the time.
Catechism. A teaching book of questions and answers on the basics of the faith. Luther's small one was written to be taught at home.

Your line: what does this mean? Today, when you catch yourself saying a familiar phrase, at church, at work or at the dinner table, ask the question once, and answer it plainly. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: Zwingli's sausages
859.hook: in Zurich, eating sausages in Lent starts a reformation
859.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep set fasts in Lent, such as abstaining from meat on certain days; some Protestant Christians fast or give something up by personal choice during Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's Small Catechism, a thin book for teaching at home. Your line was what does this mean? Which familiar phrase did you finally stop and open? Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

The presses at a print shop in Zurich have been running hard. The printer, a man named Christoph Froschauer, has a big job due, and his workers are worn out. It's Lent, the season before Easter when the church of their day forbids meat. And at a meal in the printer's house, the story goes, someone brings out sausages. They're cut up and shared around the table. A local priest is in the room. His name is Huldrych Zwingli. Word gets out, the city council gets involved, and a plate of sausages turns into a public question about the whole church. Today: Zwingli's sausages.

Here's the odd part. By the usual account, Zwingli didn't eat any. He sat at the table and let it happen. But when the eaters were accused, he stood up for them, and preached a sermon later printed as On the Choice and Freedom of Foods. His argument went to the Bible. Where, he asked, does scripture command this? He pointed to Paul, who writes in the King James Bible: "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday." Fasting, Zwingli said, can be a good thing. Anyone who wants to fast in Lent should be free to. But it shouldn't be a law that binds every conscience under threat of punishment. That's the hinge. Not a rule against fasting. A question about who gets to make the rule. And once Zurich started asking that question about sausages, it started asking it about everything else too, until the city's church was reshaped around preaching from scripture. Paul has a second line that cuts both ways, and it's worth holding next to the first. "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The eater shouldn't sneer. The faster shouldn't judge. Christians today keep Lent in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the Lenten fast together, as a discipline of the whole church. Some Protestant Christians fast by choice, or give something up. Underneath all of it is the question Zwingli raised, and it's an honest one: why do we do this?
screen: `LET NO MAN JUDGE YOU IN MEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one rule you keep without thinking. It might be a religious habit, a family custom, a way things are always done at work. Bring it to mind. Then ask Zwingli's question, gently: why do we do this? Look for the reason. Sometimes there's a good one, and the rule may mean more than it did a minute ago. Sometimes you'll find it's just habit. Either way, you'll know. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it. If you don't, just hold the rule up to the light for a while. The bell holds the time.
Zwingli's sausages. A meal in Lent in a Zurich print shop that Zwingli defended, and a question about rules that reshaped a city's church.
Your line: why do we do this? Today, ask it once out loud about something you do together with others, and listen to the answer before you change anything. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Felix Manz (1527)
860.hook: baptized as adults, an early Anabaptist martyr is drowned by other Protestants
860.howItsDone: Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite and other Anabaptist-descended churches baptize those who confess faith for themselves and remember their early martyrs, including Felix Manz, and nonviolence is part of their heritage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zwingli's sausages, and a question about rules that spread through Zurich. Your line was why do we do this? What did you find when you asked it? Day eight hundred sixty.

A small boat pushes out into the river that runs through Zurich. In it is a young man with his hands bound. His name is Felix Manz. He had studied with Zwingli, read the Bible with him, cheered the questions Zwingli raised. And he took those questions one step further than the city would allow. Now the city council of Zurich, a Protestant council in a Protestant city, has sentenced him to be drowned. The accounts say he sang as they took him out. Today's word is the name opponents gave to him and his friends: Anabaptist.
screen: `A BOAT ON THE RIVER IN ZURICH.`

segments.voice: Here's the step. Manz and a circle of friends, Conrad Grebel among them, read the New Testament and noticed that the baptisms there follow faith. People hear, believe, and then are baptized. So they asked: shouldn't baptism come after a person can confess faith for themselves? And they began baptizing one another as adults, in a house in Zurich. Their opponents called them Anabaptists, re-baptizers, because they had already been baptized as infants. They didn't accept the name. To them, this was their first real baptism. The council outlawed it. Manz was arrested, released, arrested again, and finally drowned in the river. Christians to this day answer the baptism question differently, and both answers have deep roots. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches baptize infants, seeing baptism as God's gift and promise, given before a child can ask. Mennonites, Baptists and others baptize those who confess faith themselves. But Manz's circle held something else too. They refused to take up the sword, even to defend themselves, and early Anabaptist confessions said so plainly. Their picture came from the prophet Isaiah, who sees a world where, in the King James words, "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb." And: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." The peaceable kingdom. It's a hard thing to sit with. In those years, Christians put other Christians to death over how and when to baptize. Manz was killed by a city whose reformers had once read the Bible beside him. And he went to the river still believing that followers of Jesus should never hurt anyone.
screen: `THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember those persecuted by other Christians. Start with Felix Manz in the boat. Then widen it. Anabaptists. Catholics. Protestants. Orthodox Christians. In more than one place and time, Christians have suffered at the hands of other Christians, and some still do. Hold them in mind, without needing to decide who was most to blame. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for those who hurt them. If you don't, just keep them company in silence for a while. The bell holds the time.
Anabaptist. A name opponents gave to Christians who baptized adults on their own confession of faith. Felix Manz's circle also refused the sword.
Your line: the peaceable kingdom. Today, in one argument you'd normally win by force of words, choose not to hurt. Day eight hundred sixty.

861.title: Menno Simons
861.hook: a Dutch priest who joined the Anabaptists and gave the Mennonites his name
861.howItsDone: Mennonite churches, named after Menno Simons, baptize believers, practice nonviolence and simple living, and are known for relief work such as sharing food, clothing and shelter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Felix Manz, drowned in Zurich, and the name Anabaptist. Your line was the peaceable kingdom. Where did you choose not to hurt? Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A village priest in Friesland, in the north of the Netherlands, is saying Mass. He holds up the bread, and a doubt he can't shake rises with it. He keeps his post. He keeps his comfortable life. He reads the New Testament on the side, and the doubts grow. Then news comes that a group of Anabaptists has been killed, and tradition says his own brother was among them. Men who died for what they believed, he writes, while he stayed safe and said nothing. That thought won't leave him alone. His name is Menno Simons, and a whole family of churches still carries it.

Menno left the priesthood and joined the scattered, hunted Anabaptists of the Low Countries. He didn't start their movement. He came into it, and became one of its shepherds. And he chose its peaceful side. Some who carried the Anabaptist name had turned to violence. Menno taught that Christ's followers do not take up the sword at all. From then on he lived on the move, with his family, writing and preaching and baptizing believers, with authorities hunting him. His writings carried a verse from Paul, in the King James wording: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." Everything had to stand on that. Those who followed his teaching came to be called Mennonites, after him. Then there's the passage his line comes from. In paraphrase, Menno wrote that true evangelical faith cannot lie dormant. It can't sleep. It clothes the naked. It feeds the hungry. It comforts the sorrowful. It shelters the destitute. It serves even those who harm it. It binds up what is wounded. Faith, for Menno, is something that gets up and does things. That fits with the letter of James: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." Lutheran, Catholic, Reformed and Mennonite teachers put faith and works together in different ways. But Menno's list is practical enough for anyone. It's about bread and blankets. And it came from a man who spent years with nowhere safe to sleep.

Here's the practice: live simply today. Settle and breathe. Then look honestly at your day ahead. Is there one thing you could do without? A purchase you don't need. A second helping. An hour of scrolling. And is there one thing on Menno's list you could do instead? Clothes you no longer wear, set aside to give. Food for someone hungry. A word for someone sad. fork.setup: you're Menno, a priest with a safe life and growing doubts. news comes that Anabaptists, your brother among them, have died for their faith. what do you do?
options: keep your post and your doubts to yourself.
leave the priesthood and join the hunted Anabaptists.
join the Anabaptists who have taken up arms.
fork.reveal: he left his post, joined the peaceful Anabaptists, and spent years on the move, hunted, writing that true faith cannot lie dormant.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mennonites are named after a place.
what it means: they're named after Menno Simons, a priest who joined the Anabaptists and taught a faith without the sword.
what a scholar hears: Menno set 1 Corinthians 3:11 at the heart of his writing, and wrote that true evangelical faith cannot lie dormant but clothes, feeds, comforts and shelters.
